worksheet.title: Order Matters
worksheet.subtitle: Same blocks, different order, different number
worksheet.learning_goal: I can show how the order of the blocks changes the result.

parts.title: The path has ends
parts.text: Bit's path ends at 5. Bit cannot go past 5 — if a forward block would go past the end, Bit STOPS on 5. (Bit cannot go below 0 either.) Because of this, the ORDER of the blocks can change where Bit lands.

parts.title: Run Code 1
parts.prompt: Start on 3. Forward 3 would pass the end, so Bit stops on 5. Then back 1. What number does Bit land on? Write it.

parts.title: Predict, then run Code 2
parts.prompt: PREDICT first: where will Bit land? Then run Code 2 from 3: back 1, then forward 3. What number does Bit land on?

parts.title: You try — think and build
parts.prompt: (a) Code 1 and Code 2 use the SAME blocks. Did Bit land on the same number? Circle YES or NO, and tell why. (b) Write an order of these three blocks that lands Bit on 5.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: The blocks run in order from the top. The same blocks in a different order can give a different result — so the order of your code matters.

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students run two programs built from the SAME blocks in a different order and find that Bit lands on different numbers, then describe why and build their own order to a target. This is reading and altering code and describing how the change affects the outcome (C3.2), with a write-your-own step (C3.1).

parts.title: Ontario curriculum (Grade 1 — C3 Coding)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: The printed worksheet and a pencil. Optional: a floor number path 0-5 so students can walk both codes and feel Bit stop at the end (5).

parts.title: Run it (about 20 min)
text: 1. I DO: walk Code 1 — 'start at 3… forward 3 would be 6, but the path ends at 5, so Bit stops on 5… back 1 to 4.'
2. WE DO: Exercise 1 — Code 1 lands on 4. Exercise 2 — predict Code 2, then run: back 1 to 2, forward 3 to 5.
3. YOU DO: Exercise 3 — same blocks landed on different numbers (4 vs 5); students explain why and write an order that reaches 5.
4. Connect: 'Computers run code in the exact order you give it. Change the order and you can change what happens.'

parts.title: Answer key (modelled by the run-gate)
text: Ex 1 — Code 1: 3 → forward 3 stops at 5 → back 1 → 4.

Ex 3 — (a) NO, not the same (4 vs 5). Why it works that way: in Code 1 the forward 3 happens at 3 and runs into the end of the path, so Bit stops at 5 and 'loses' a step; in Code 2 Bit steps back first, so forward 3 fits without hitting the end. (b) Any order that reaches 5, e.g. 'start at 3, back 1, forward 3' (the Code 2 order).

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common idea: students expect 3 + 3 − 1 to always be 5; the edge of the path is what makes the order matter — model it on the floor path.
Simplify: do Code 1 and Code 2 side by side on the floor path so the different landings are felt, not just calculated.
Extend: ask for an order of the blocks that lands Bit on 4, and whether more than one order can reach the same number.
Success indicator: the child lands Code 1 on 4 and Code 2 on 5 and explains that the order changed the result.
